content: The homicide rate in Brazil more than doubled during the analyzed period. Since 2001, Brazilian authorities have implemented various measures to reduce homicides, including a law restricting gun ownership and prohibiting civilians, except police and armed forces members, from carrying firearms. Despite these efforts, homicides among adolescents and young adults remain a significant public health issue, necessitating additional prevention strategies targeting this demographic. Data for this analysis were sourced from Brazil's Mortality Information System, which compiles death certificate information from all states. Additional data for São Paulo city were obtained from the Program for Quality Improvement of Mortality Information. Homicide was defined as death resulting from intentional injury inflicted by another person, including legal interventions, with underlying causes coded according to the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) Ninth and Tenth Revisions. Population data for Brazil and São Paulo city were retrieved from BGSI. Crude, age-specific, and sex-specific homicide rates were calculated per 100,000 population. To explore the relationship between socioeconomic status and homicide rates in São Paulo city, data on the monthly average income of household heads from the 2000 Brazil Population Census were analyzed using Pearson correlation. Brazil had one of the highest global homicide rates in 2002, nearly four times that of the United States. In 2000, Brazil accounted for an estimated 28% of all homicides in the Americas, a region with the highest homicide rate. Contributing factors to increased violence include urbanization, illegal drug and firearms trafficking, economic crises, unemployment, and income inequality. A strong negative correlation between income and homicide rates in São Paulo aligns with findings from other urban areas worldwide. Further research is needed to understand the link between violence and poverty to develop effective interventions. Brazil has adopted measures to reduce homicides. In 2001, the Ministry of Health issued a national policy to reduce injury-related morbidity and mortality. In 2002, guidelines for reporting child maltreatment by health professionals were introduced. In December 2003, the Brazilian Congress passed a law controlling gun ownership, prohibiting civilians from carrying firearms, and imposing stricter penalties for international firearms trafficking. São Paulo state implemented an injury surveillance system in 2002, and improved surveillance data can guide program and policy design to reduce violence. Several violence-prevention initiatives have been developed in Brazil. In Rio de Janeiro, the NGO Viva Rio promotes firearm risk awareness, reduces firearm injuries, fosters peace, and provides vocational training for impoverished youth. In São Paulo state, a coalition of private sector groups, state banking organizations, media companies, and research centers established the São Paulo Institute Against Violence to support violence prevention projects. São Paulo city implemented the Renda Minima Program, offering financial support to low-income families, and the Bolsa Trabalho Program, promoting youth employment. These programs may help reduce homicide rates, and their impact should be evaluated to guide interventions in other communities. The findings in this report are subject to limitations. Death certificate data may underestimate firearm-related homicides. Studies based on medical examiner records in large Brazilian cities, such as Recife, show that over 90% of homicides involve firearms, whereas death certificates indicate less than 70%. A planned homicide surveillance system in São Paulo city will link death certificate data with medical examiner and police records to inform public policies. Hypothermia, defined as a core body temperature below 95°F (35°C), causes approximately 600 deaths annually in the United States. Exposure to excessive cold slows enzymatic activity, potentially leading to fatal rhabdomyolysis, coagulopathy, renal failure, and dysrhythmias. Modifiable factors associated with hypothermia include alcohol intake, activity level, and clothing type. Understanding the epidemiology and pathophysiology of hypothermia is crucial for prevention. Three fatal hypothermia cases from 2003 illustrate the risks. Case 1 involved a 44-year-old man found outdoors in Vermont with wet clothing and an empty vodka bottle nearby. The temperature had dropped below freezing overnight, and his death was attributed to hypothermia with alcohol intoxication as a contributing factor. Case 2 involved a 76-year-old man with Alzheimer’s disease found in a swampy area in Vermont after his car became stuck. The temperature had dropped below freezing, and his death was due to hypothermia caused by a cold, wet environment. Case 3 involved a 35-year-old hiker in Alaska found along a highway in wet, windy conditions. His death was attributed to hypothermia, with drug and alcohol intoxication as contributing factors. Populations at increased risk for hypothermia include the elderly, homeless, chronically ill, alcoholics, drug users, and those with preexisting heart disease. In 2001, 599 deaths in the U.S. were attributed to excessive natural cold exposure, with 67% of victims being male and 51% aged over 65 years. Advanced age, immobility, and medical conditions increase hypothermia risk. Alcohol and drug use impair judgment, mobility, and decision-making, further increasing risk. Treatment of hypothermia focuses on rewarming the core body temperature and providing supportive care. Prevention requires public health strategies targeting at-risk populations, such as community programs to check on the elderly, temporary shelters for the homeless, and advice for individuals with cardiovascular disease to avoid outdoor exercise during cold weather. Alcohol abuse is the third leading preventable cause of death in the U.S., associated with cirrhosis, cancer, heart disease, stroke, injury, and depression. Public health efforts aim to reduce binge and heavy drinking. In New Hampshire, alcohol use trends among adolescents and adults were analyzed using data from the Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS), Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), and Vital Records. Binge drinking was defined as consuming five or more drinks on one occasion, and heavy drinking as an average daily consumption exceeding two drinks for men and one for women. In 2003, 26.6% of New Hampshire adults reported binge drinking, and 6.3% reported heavy drinking. Among adolescents, 26.6% reported binge drinking. Interventions are needed to prevent adolescent drinking and reduce excessive alcohol use among adults. Limitations of the report include underestimation of binge drinking prevalence, lack of trend analysis for high school students, and limited analysis of alcohol-related health effects beyond chronic liver disease. New Hampshire plans to update alcohol surveillance data annually to guide prevention programs.
